<h1 style="text-align: center"> **Overview** </h1>
<br>
<h2 style="text-align: center"> **Executive Summary** </h2>

<div style="border: 1px solid #000; padding: 10px; background-color: #FDECEF;">
<span style="font-size: 15px; font-weight: 800;">**Background**</span><br>
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are widespread, persistent synthetic chemicals used in many consumer and industrial products. Prenatal exposure has been linked to adverse health outcomes, but the biological mechanisms underlying these associations are unclear. Untargeted metabolomics can profile thousands of small molecules (metabolites) in blood, offering a way to identify early-life biochemical changes associated with prenatal PFAS exposure.

<div style="border-left: 3px solid #000; padding: 15px; background-color: #F8BBD0; margin-top: 10px;">

<span style="font-size: 15px; font-weight: 800;">**Objective**</span><br>
**Identify cord-serum metabolomic features and metabolic pathways associated with prenatal PFAS exposure to understand how prenatal exposure to PFAS may influence early-life biology.** 
</div>

<br><span style="font-size: 15px; font-weight: 800;">**Data**</span><br>
264 mother–infant dyads were analyzed in the HOME Study. Prenatal serum PFAS were measured at ~16 weeks’ gestation (*primary*: PFOS, PFOA, PFHxS, PFNA, *secondary*: MeFOSAA). Cord serum was profiled using LC-HRMS, yielding 14,402 metabolomic features (ions). Features were putatively annotated using the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB). 

<span style="font-size: 15px; font-weight: 800;">**Approach**</span><br>
<u>Metabolome Wide Association Study (MWAS)</u>*
<ul style="margin-top: 6px; margin-bottom: 0;">
<li>*4-PFAS Mixture (primary)*: Adjusted quantile-based g-computation to estimate the joint effect of the 4-PFAS mixture on each metabolomic feature.
</li>

<li>*Single-pollutant MWAS (secondary)*: Covariate-adjusted linear models for each PFAS individually to contextualize mixture results and identify PFAS-specific signals.
</li></ul>

<br><u>*mummichog* Pathway Enrichment Analysis (PEA):</u> The primary MWAS outputs were used in a *mummichog* PEA to identify biological pathways most consistently implicated by PFAS exposure.

<u>Sensitivity analysis:</u> Re-ran the mixture MWAS with MeFOSAA added (5-PFAS mixture) and repeated *mummichog* pathway enrichment to assess the robustness of the primary findings.

<span style="font-size: 15px; font-weight: 800;">**Key Results**</span><br>
The 4-PFAS mixture was associated with 4 cord-serum metabolic features (FDR < 0.20): PFOS, PFHxS, a putatively identified thyroid-related metabolite (3-monoiodo-L-thyronine 4-O-sulfate), and one unidentified feature (m/z 590.0020; RT 441.4 s). 

Pathway enrichment linked the 4-PFAS-mixture to 49 metabolic pathways (p < 0.05), with strongest representation in amino acid, carbohydrate, lipid, cofactor/vitamin metabolism, and glycan biosynthesis/metabolism. Several pathways were consistently enriched across mixture and single-PFAS results (e.g., TCA cycle, keratan sulfate degradation, phytanic acid peroxisomal oxidation), pointing to common metabolic themes. 

Adding MeFOSAA (5-PFAS mixture) produced similar pathway-enrichment patterns, supporting the robustness of the primary findings.
<br>

<div style="border-left: 3px solid #000; padding: 10px 10px; background-color: #F8BBD0; margin-top: 10px;">
<span style="font-size: 15px; font-weight: 800;">**Why this matters**</span><br>
These results point to plausible biological mechanisms linking prenatal PFAS exposure to altered neonatal metabolism. Next steps include formal mediation analyses to evaluate whether these pathways help explain PFAS associations with outcomes such as birthweight or vaccine response.
</div>
</div>
<br>
**\*Notes**
<br>*Multiple-testing control:* A false discovery rate correction (FDR &lt;0.2; Benjamini–Hochberg) was applied across MWAS results to account for thousands of tests.
<br>*Covariates adjustments:* maternal age, race/ethnicity, parity, household income, and cotinine concentrations (smoking).
<br><br>**Implementation**<br> Analyses were implemented in R using modular scripts/functions to support reproducibility and consistent analysis across thousands of features. Key outputs include MWAS and pathway-enrichment visualizations, plus sensitivity analyses evaluating robustness to mixture specification.
<br><br>**Reproducibility**<br> HOME Study data is restricted; this project emphasizes transparent, modular analysis code and reproducible figure generation.
<br>
<br>

<h2 style="text-align: center"><b>Data Access & Running the Code</b></h2>

<span style="font-size: 15px; font-weight: 800;">Data Access Note.</span>
The data for this study is from the Health Outcomes and Measures of the Environment (HOME) Study [(Braun et al.)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27006352/). This data is not publicly available. However, the HOME Study principal investigators are actively engaged in collaborative data-sharing projects and welcome new collaborations. Interested investigators can request data access here [(HOME Study Data Request)](https://homestudy.research.cchmc.org/contact). The HOME Study Data Sharing Committee meets regularly to review proposed research projects, ensure that they do not overlap with existing projects, and ensure efficient use of limited resources (e.g., cord blood). <br>

<span style="font-size: 15px; font-weight: 800;">How to Run the Analysis</span>
<ol>
  <li>
    Open the <code>.Rmd</code> and set your local paths (or update <code>root.dir</code>) so the project can find the analysis-ready inputs.
  </li>
  <li>
    Run sections in order:
    <ol style="margin-top: 6px; margin-left: 22px;">
      <li>Data Import & Data Cleaning</li>
      <li>Metabolome Wide Association Study (MWAS)</li>
      <li>Pathway Enrichment Analysis (PEA)</li>
    </ol>
  </li>
  <li>
    MWAS outputs are written to <b>Final Datasets/</b> (full results, significant-only results, and MetaboAnalyst/*mummichog* input files).
  </li>
  <li>
    Pathway enrichment outputs (*mummichog* results) are saved as <code>.csv</code> files for mixture, single-PFAS, and sensitivity analyses.
  </li>
</ol>


<span style="font-size: 15px; font-weight: 800;">Notes for Reuse.</span>
This workflow can be adapted to other metabolomics MWAS settings by updating:
<ul>
<li>exposure names (PFAS variables),</li>
<li>covariates included in the models, and</li>
<li>file paths for imports/exports.</li>
</ul>
<br>

<h2 style="text-align: center"><b>Repository Overview</b></h2>

<div class="repo-overview"><p>
This repository provides a reproducible, end-to-end workflow for conducting a metabolome-wide association study (MWAS) of prenatal PFAS exposures and interpreting feature-level results using <em>mummichog</em> pathway enrichment. It supports my first-author, peer-reviewed publication <a href="https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acs.est.3c07515" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">(Hall et al.)</a> and is designed as an instructional resource for researchers replicating MWAS + <em>mummichog</em> pipelines.
</p>

<p>This workflow begins from <strong>analysis-ready inputs</strong> (i.e., after upstream LC&ndash;HRMS processing and study-specific QC). Upstream processing steps are summarized in Figure 1 below for transparency but are not re-run here.
</p>
</div>

knitr::include_graphics("Figures/workflow_end_to_end.png")

<h2 style="text-align: center"><b>Workflow & Deliverables</b></h2>
<div style="border: 1px solid #000; padding: 10px; background-color: #FDECEF">
<br><br>
<h3 style="font-weight: 800;">Analysis Code</h3>
<span style="font-size: 15px; font-weight: 800;">1. Data Import & Cleaning</span>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  Cleans and structures data for analyses.
</div>
<br>
<span style="font-size: 15px; font-weight: 800;">2. Metabolome Wide Association Study (MWAS)</span>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <u>Section 2.1</u> Conducts an MWAS using quantile-based g-computation
  (<a href="https://ehp.niehs.nih.gov/doi/full/10.1289/EHP5838">Keil et al.</a>).
  This evaluates associations between a 4-PFAS mixture (PFOS, PFOA, PFNA, PFHxS)
  and each cord serum metabolite.
</div>
<br>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <u>Section 2.2</u> Conducts an MWAS using linear regression to identify
  individual associations between each PFAS and each metabolite. The purpose
  of this analysis was to contextualize mixture results and identify
  PFAS-specific signals.
</div>
<br>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <u>Section 2.3</u> Conducts an MWAS using quantile-based g-computation to
  evaluate associations between a 5-PFAS mixture (4-PFAS mixture plus MeFOSAA)
  and each metabolite. This serves as a sensitivity analysis to assess the
  impact of MeFOSAA on the primary findings.
</div>
<br>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <em>Note:</em> These analyses use the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate
  (BH FDR). An FDR &lt; 0.20 was used as an exploratory threshold to retain a
  broader set of candidate metabolic features for follow-up investigation.
</div>
<br>
<span style="font-size: 15px; font-weight: 800;">3. Pathway Enrichment Analysis (PEA)</span>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <u>Section 3.2</u> Performs a PEA using <em>mummichog</em> via MetaboAnalyst 3.2
  to identify pathways associated with the 4-PFAS mixture (PFOS, PFOA, PFNA,
  PFHxS) (<a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23861661/">Li et al.</a>).
  Input data were generated during the 4-PFAS MWAS (Section 2.1).
</div>
<br>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <u>Section 3.3</u> Performs a PEA using <em>mummichog</em> via MetaboAnalyst 3.2
  for each individual PFAS. Input data were generated during the single-PFAS
  MWAS (Section 2.2) to evaluate PFAS-specific pathway patterns relative to the
  mixture.
</div>
<br>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <u>Section 3.4</u> Performs a PEA using <em>mummichog</em> via MetaboAnalyst 3.2
  for a 5-PFAS mixture. Input data were generated during the 5-PFAS MWAS
  (Section 2.3) as a sensitivity analysis to assess robustness to mixture
  specification.
</div>
<br>
<h3 style="font-weight: 800;">Figures and Table Code</h3>
<span style="font-size: 15px; font-weight: 800;">4. Exploratory Data Analysis</span>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <u>Section 4.1</u> Displays a PFAS correlation heatmap (Spearman correlations;
  upper triangle only; coefficients labeled) based on non–log-transformed
  maternal serum PFAS concentrations (PFOS, PFOA, PFNA, PFHxS, MeFOSAA) to
  summarize correlation structure across compounds.
</div>
<br>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <u>Section 4.2</u> Displays PFAS violin plots with boxplot overlays to visualize
  the distribution of prenatal PFAS concentrations. Because PFAS concentrations
  differ substantially in scale, a median (IQR) table is included beneath the
  figure to aid interpretation.
</div>
<br>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <u>Section 4.3</u> Displays a descriptive Table 1 summarizing maternal and
  household characteristics in the HOME Study (2003–2006), with continuous
  variables reported as medians (IQR) and categorical variables reported as
  N (%).
</div>
<br>
<span style="font-size: 15px; font-weight: 800;">5. Metabolome Wide Association Study (MWAS) – Figures</span>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <u>Section 5.1</u> Displays MWAS results for a 4-PFAS mixture using volcano
  plots to visualize effect estimates and statistical evidence across cord
  serum metabolites.
</div>
<br>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <u>Section 5.2</u> Displays MWAS results for each individual PFAS using volcano
  plots, enabling comparison of PFAS-specific signals with mixture-based
  results.
</div>
<br>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <u>Section 5.3</u> Displays sensitivity-analysis MWAS results for a 5-PFAS
  mixture using volcano plots to assess whether inclusion of MeFOSAA alters
  overall patterns of association.
</div>
<br>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  Volcano plots were originally developed by <strong>Elvira Fleury</strong> and edited by <strong>Amber Hampton</strong>.
</div>
<br>
<span style="font-size: 15px; font-weight: 800;">6. Pathway Enrichment Analysis (PEA) – Figures</span>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <u>Section 6.1</u> Displays pathway enrichment results for the 4-PFAS mixture
  as well as individual PFAS using bubble plots summarizing pathway-level signals.
</div>
<br>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <u>Section 6.2</u> Displays sensitivity-analysis pathway enrichment results for
  a 5-PFAS mixture, enabling pathway-level comparison with the primary
  4-PFAS mixture.
</div>
<br>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  <u>Section 6.3</u> Displays a pathway overlap Venn diagram comparing individual PFAS-specific pathway
  signals.
</div>
<br>
<div style="margin-left: 1.2em;">
  Bubble plot figures and Venn diagram were originally developed by <strong>Elvira Fleury</strong> and edited by <strong>Amber Hampton</strong>.
</div>
</div>

<br>

<h1 style="text-align: center"> **Analysis Code** </h1>

<h2 style="text-align: center"> **1. Data Import & Data Cleaning** </h2>

<h3 style="text-align: center"> 1.1. Needed Libraries </h3>

I first secured all needed packages if I did not have these installed already; this step is required before you can run this code. An example of code to install a package in R is as follows:    
<br>
<div style="border: padding: 10px; width: 250px;">
    install.packages("tidyverse")
</div>

where "tidyverse" can be replaced with any of the packages in the code block below except for MetaboanalystR. MetaboanalystR installation instructions can be found here [(MetaboAnalystR)](https://www.metaboanalyst.ca/docs/RTutorial.xhtml#2.%20Analysis%20Utilities).   
<br>
After all packages are appropriately installed, load all necessary packages using the code below.

```{r Libraries,, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#Creating an object named libraries with all of the packages I want to load
libraries <- c("knitr", "tidyverse", "qgcomp", "ggpubr", "MetaboAnalystR", "fitdistrplus", "RJSONIO", "ggplot2", "reshape2", 'grid', 'ggvenn')

#Loading the packages and suppressing all error messages and the function return value
invisible(sapply(libraries, library, character.only = TRUE))
```

<h3 style="text-align: center"> 1.2. Data Import </h3>

After loading all the needed packages, I then imported all of my data. I started with my metabolomics data. This is the focus of the code chunk below.    

For this code chunk I have 2 sets of files:
<br>
  <ul><li>The main C18 and HILIC files (named *C18* and *HILIC*)</li>
  <li>The map C18 and HILIC files (named *C18_map* and *HILIC_map*)</li></ul>
The main files contain feature data (mass to charge ratios (*mz*), retention time, and ion abundances) for each feature for each participant. The map files contain the participant IDs and the metabolomic-specific IDs for each participant. The metabolomic-specific IDs are used in the main *C18* and *HILIC* files where all other imported files use the participant IDs.   

<br>
For the main files, the headers are detailed in the box below.    

<div style="border: 1px solid #000; padding: 10px">
<h5 style="text-align: center"> **Main File Headers**</h5> 
<h6 style="text-align: center">**Dataframe Names: **<b><i>C18</i></b> **and** <b><i>HILIC</i></b></h6>
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px"> <u>column 1</u>. *mz*: the mass to charge ratio.
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px"> <u>column 2</u>. *time*: retention time.
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px"> <u>column 3</u>. *mode*: labeled 1 for C18 and 2 for HILIC files.   
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px"> <u>column 4+</u>. a column for each participant containing the the feature data. There are likely several hundred to several thousand metabolic features 
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 100px">that have been identified. The header name for each row is the metabolomic-specific ID (which differs from the participant. 
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 100px"> ID). An example of a metabolomics specific ID is *C18_105*.
  </p><br>
*The number of columns in the main files are equal to the number of participants + 3*
</div>
<br>  


For the map files, the headers are detailed in the box below.   

<div style="border: 1px solid #000; padding: 10px">
<h5 style="text-align: center">**Map File Headers**</h5>
<h6 style="text-align: center">**Dataframe Names: **<b><i>C18_map</i></b> **and** <b><i>HILIC_map</i></b></h6>
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px"> <u>column 1</u>. *participant_ID*: The assigned participant ID for the data in this study.
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px"> <u>column 2</u>. *HILIC_ID* for HILIC data and *C18_ID* for C18 data. IDs that are specific only to the metabolomics data. 
  </p>
</div>
<br>
<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;">
  <div style="border: 1px solid #000; padding: 10px; background-color: #F8BBD0; width: 500px">
  <div style="text-align: left; text-indent: 10px">
<h4 style="text-align: center">**IMPORTANT**</h4> 
<h5 style="text-align: center">**For this study, I performed the following pre-analysis processing steps for both HILIC and C18 data:**</h5>   
  </div>
  <ul>
  <li>Batch corrected using WaveICA 2.0 [(Deng et al.)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34542717/) </li>
  <li>Removed if CV >30% (within triplicate) </li>
  <li>Removed values when non-detect intensities >20% </li>
  <li>Imputed missing values using:   
  <br>
  $\begin{aligned}\small\frac{\text{the minimum value per feature}}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$
  </li>
  <li>Features were log2 transformed </li>
  </div>
  </div>
<br>
Next, I imported the feature data and map files using the code chunk below. 
<br>
```{r Import_Feature}
# Importing the C18 map file that identifies the IDs
C18_map <- read.csv("Data/C18_map_clean.csv", header = TRUE) # INSERT YOUR FILE PATHWAY HERE

# Importing the HILIC map file that identifies the IDs

# Importing the batch-corrected C18 data
C18 <- read.csv ('Data/C18_clean.csv', header = TRUE) # INSERT YOUR FILE PATHWAY HERE

# Importing the batch-corrected HILIC data
HILIC <- read.csv ('Data/HILIC_clean.csv', header = TRUE) # INSERT YOUR FILE PATHWAY HERE
```

After importing the feature and PFAS data, I imported the covariate data. This dataset was named *cov*.

For *cov*, the headers are as follows:

<div style="border: 1px solid #000; padding: 10px">
<h5 style="text-align: center">**Covariate Dataset Headers**</h5>
<h6 style="text-align: center">**Dataframe Name: **<b><i>cov</i></b></h6>
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px"> <u>column 1.</u> *participant_ID*: The assigned participant ID for the data in this study.

```{r Import_Covariate}
# Importing covariate data
cov <- read.csv("Data/covariates_clean.csv", header = TRUE) # INSERT YOUR FILE PATHWAY HERE
```

<h3 style="text-align: center"> 1.3. Creating a Master Dataset</h3>
<br>
<h4 style="text-align: center">Exposure Variables and Covariates</h4>

The purpose of this code was to create a master dataset named *pfas*. I did this by merging the following datasets into a single dataset:

1.  *pfas_only*: PFAS data
2.  *cov*: covariate data
3.  *C18_map*: contains metabolomic-specific IDs and participant IDs for the C18 data
4.  *HILIC_map*: contains metabolomic-specific IDs and participant IDs for the HILIC data

This is seen below. 

```{r Master_Dataset}
# Creating a 'master' PFAS dataset called 'pfas' with both pfas and covariate information
pfas <- pfas_only %>%
  merge(cov, by = "participant_ID") %>%
  merge(C18_map, by = "participant_ID") %>%
  merge(HILIC_map, by = "participant_ID")
```
<br>

<h4 style="text-align: center">Feature Table</h4>

Next, I created a new dataframe named *feature_table*. *feature_table* contains only participants with both PFAS and covariate data (i.e. is a subset of the full dataframe; this is for a complete case analysis). This feature table also contains both C18 and HILIC data stacked on top of one another. Columns for the new feature table can be seen below.

<div style="border: 1px solid #000; padding: 10px">
<h5 style="text-align: center"> **Feature Table Headers**</h5> 
<h6 style="text-align: center">**Dataframe Name: **<b><i>feature_table</i></b></h6>
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px;"> <u>column 1.</u> *mz*: the mass to charge ratio.
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px;"> <u>column 2.</u> *time*: retention time.
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px;"> <u>column 3.</u> labeled 1 for C18 and 2 for HILIC files. 
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px;"> <u>column 4.</u> a column for each participant containing the ion abundance for each metabolite (referred to as a 'feature'). The header name for 
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 100px;"> each row is the participant ID. An example of a participant ID is 'C18_1'.  
<br>
*The number of columns in the new dataframe is equal to the number of participants + 3.*
</div>
<br>
Below is the code I used to create this feature table. 
<br>
```{r Feature_Table}
# Creating a 'participant' file that is a list of participants. 
participants <- unique(pfas["participant_ID"])

# Join the C18_map data frame to the participants data frame 
participants <- inner_join(participants, C18_map, by = "participant_ID")

# Join the HILIC_map data frame to the participants data frame
participants <- inner_join(participants, HILIC_map, by = "participant_ID")

#Creating a string of characters called 'C18_ID' that contain all of the metabolomic-specific IDs for C18 as well as mz, rt, and mode
C18_ID <- c("mz", "time", "mode", participants$C18_ID)
  
# Selecting only participants from the C18 file that contain both pfas and covariate information
C18 <- subset(C18, select = C18_ID)

#Creating a general metabolomics-specific ID rather than one specific for C18 data
    #As of now participant 1 will correspond to both C18_1 and HILIC_1. Here I drop the C18 portion and replace it with ID changing the value to ID_1. This will allow me to stack the HILIC and C18 data ontop of one another.  
colnames(C18) <- gsub("C18","ID", colnames(C18)) 
  
#Creating a list called 'HILIC_ID' that contain all of the metabolomic-specific IDs for HILIC as well as mz, rt, and mode
HILIC_ID <- c("mz", "time", "mode", participants$HILIC_ID)

# Selecting only participants from the HILIC file that contain both pfas and covariate information
HILIC <- subset(HILIC, select = HILIC_ID)

#Creating a general metabolomics-specific ID rather than one specific for HILIC data
colnames(HILIC) <- gsub("HILIC","ID", colnames(HILIC))
  
# Creating a 'master' dataframe called 'feature' with both the C18 and HILIC data stacked on top of one another
feature_table <- bind_rows(C18, HILIC)  
```

<h3 style="text-align: center"> 1.4. Splitting Data for Analysis </h3>

The purpose of this chunk was to create a list that 'splits' each individual feature into their own tibble. Each individual tibble contains the mass-to-charge ratio (*mz*) and retention time (*time*) for that metabolite as well as the pfas and covariate data for each participant. The purpose of doing this is so that I could run each individual metabolite independently through the MWAS.

```{r Splitting_For_Analysis}
# Adding a new feature column named 'feature_id'. This columns contains numbers 1,2,3,...N. This column will be used later for splitting the feature table
feature_table <- cbind(feature_id = 1:nrow(feature_table), feature_table)

# Pivoting the dataset to a 'long file'. This contains 6 values (feature_ID, mz, time, mode, name [metabolomic-specific participant_ID], and value [ion abundance]). 
long_df <- feature_table %>% pivot_longer(!c(1:4))

# Replacing the C18 value names to a general ID to match the long_df
pfas <- pfas  %>%
  mutate(C18_ID = str_replace(C18_ID, "C18", "ID")) #Dropping the C18 to merge with the long dataset

# Creating a long feature table to analyze
analysis_pfas <- inner_join(long_df, pfas, by= c("name"= "C18_ID"))
split_pfas <- split(analysis_pfas, f=analysis_pfas$feature_id)
```
<br>

<h2 style="text-align: center"> **2. Metabolome Wide Association Study**</h2>

<h3 style="text-align: center"> 2.0. Brief Background: QGComp </h3>
The purpose of quantile-based g-computation (QGComp) is to examine the joint effects of a mixture PFAS with relation to an outcome of interest. QGComp accomplishes this by calculating the parameters of a marginal structural model. For the QGComp models in this study, these parameters characterize the difference in feature intensity resulting from a simultaneous, one-quantile increase of all PFAS in the mixture. Resources on quantile-based g-computation are in the box below.   

<br>
<div style="border: 1px solid #000; padding: 10px; background-color: #FDECEF">
<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;">
  <div style="text-align: left; text-indent: 10px">
<h5>**Resources for QGComp:**</h5>   
  </div>
  <ul>
  <li>The original paper [(Keil et al.)](https://ehp.niehs.nih.gov/doi/full/10.1289/EHP5838).</li>
  <li>Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) [(Cran website)](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/qgcomp/).</li>
  <li>Github page [(QGComp Github)](https://github.com/alexpkeil1/qgcomp)
  </ul>
</div>
</div>
<div>
<br>
</div>
<h3 style="text-align: center"> 2.1. 4-PFAS Mixture MWAS</h3>
This chunk of code is the primary Metabolome Wide Association Study (MWAS) analysis for my study  [(Hall et al.)](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acs.est.3c07515). I evaluate whether the joint effect of the 4 PFAS of interest (PFOS, PFOA, PFHxS, PFNA) were associated with the ion abundance for each feature, adjusting for parity, family income, maternal age, maternal race, and cotinine concentrations (e.g. smoking). 

The results of these models are outputted to 3 files, detailed in the box below. 

<div style="border: 1px solid #000; padding: 10px">
<h5 style="text-align: center"> **Files Outputted from the 4-PFAS MWAS Code**</h5> 
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px"> <u>File 1</u>:* a full or overall file that contains all the results
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px"> <u>File 2</u>: a significant file that contains significant values (i.e. those with FDR values <0.20)
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px"> <u>File 3</u>:* a metaboanalyst file that contains only the variables needed to import into metaboanalyst (*mz*, *time*, *p-value*, *mode*).   
  <br>
*Files 1 and 3 contain 9 columns. These columns are:
  <ol>
  <li>*m.z*: the mass to charge ratio </li>
  <li>*r.t*: retention time </li>
  <li>*psi*: effect estimate for the joint effects of these 4 PFAS. For this model, psi represents the difference in feature intensity resulting from a simultaneous, one-quantile increase of all PFAS in the mixture </li>
  <li>*SE*: standard error </li>
  <li>*ci_lower*: lower 95% confidence interval</li>
  <li>*ci_upper*: upper 95% confidence interval</li>
  <li>*p.value*: unadjusted p-value (before FDR correction)</li> 
  <li>*mode*: negative (C18) or positive (HILIC)</li> 
  <li>*FDR*: false discovery rate (FDR) corrected p-value</li>
</div>
<br>
**For the code below, you will need to specify your own file pathways to export the results. Furthermore, if you are adjusting for covariates, you will need to update the variables in the code below**. *value* in this code refers to the ion abundance of each feature. 

```{r QGComp_4_PFAS}
# Creating a list of exposure names
Xnm <- c("pfoa_log2","pfos_log2","pfna_log2","pfhxs_log2")

# Writing a function that loops through each individual features and runs quantile-based g-computation, adjusting for covariates.
find_psi_4PFAS <- function(list) {
  num_metabolites <- length(list)
  res_mat <- matrix(NA, nrow = num_metabolites, ncol = 8)
  colnames(res_mat) <- c("m.z", "r.t", "psi", "SE", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p.value", "mode")
  for (i in 1:num_metabolites) {
    data_matrix <- as.matrix(list[[i]])
    # Quantile-based g-computation model
    res <- qgcomp.noboot(value ~ midincome + mom_race + momagedeliv + ct_16w + parity +
                           pfoa_log2 + pfos_log2 + pfna_log2 + pfhxs_log2,
                         expnms = Xnm, data = list[[i]], family = gaussian())
    # Outputting needed values
    res_mat[i, 1] <- as.numeric(list[[i]][1, 2]) # mz
    res_mat[i, 2] <- as.numeric(list[[i]][1, 3]) # time ie. r.t
    res_mat[i, 3] <- as.numeric(res$psi) # psi
    res_mat[i,4] <- as.numeric((res$ci[2]-res$ci[1])/3.92) #SE
    res_mat[i, 5:6] <- res$ci # upper and lower confidence interval
    res_mat[i, 7] <- as.numeric(res$pval[2]) # p-value
    res_mat[i, 8] <- as.numeric(list[[i]][1, 4]) # mode
  }

  # Applying the False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction
  res_df <- data.frame(res_mat)
  res_df$FDR <- p.adjust(res_df$p.value, method = 'BH')
  # Re-coding mode to 'negative' and 'positive'
  res_df$mode[res_df$mode == 1] <- "negative"
  res_df$mode[res_df$mode == 2] <- "positive"
  return(res_df)
}

# Creating files
qg_comp_4_FULL <- suppressWarnings(as.data.frame(find_psi_4PFAS(split_pfas)))
qg_comp_4_SIG <- qg_comp_4_FULL[qg_comp_4_FULL$FDR< 0.2,]
qg_comp_4_METABOANALYST <- subset(qg_comp_4_FULL, select=c("m.z", "p.value","r.t", "mode"))
```

<h3 style="text-align: center"> 2.2. Single Pollutant MWAS</h3>

The code chunk below evaluates whether each individual PFAS (PFOS, PFOA, PFHxS, PFNA, or MeFOSAA) is associated with the ion abundance for each feature, adjusting for parity, family income, maternal age, maternal race, and cotinine concentrations. The purpose of this was to observe the potential impact of the individual metabolites on the 4-PFAS mixture (detailed in Section 2.1).   

The results of these models are outputted to 3 files, detailed in the box below.

<div style="border: 1px solid #000; padding: 10px">
<h5 style="text-align: center"> **Files Outputted from the Single Pollutant PFAS MWAS Code**</h5> 
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px"> <u>File 1</u>:* a full or overall file that contains all the results
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px"> <u>File 2</u>: a significant file that contains significant values (i.e. those with FDR values <0.20)
  <p style="margin: 0; text-indent: 25px"> <u>File 3</u>:* a metaboanalyst file that contains only the variables needed to import into metaboanalyst (*mz*, *time*, *p-value*, *mode*).   
  <br>
*Files 1 and 3 contain 9 columns. These columns are:
  <ol>
  <li>*m.z*: the mass to charge ratio </li>
  <li>*r.t*: retention time </li>
  <li>*psi*: effect estimate for the joint effects of these 4 PFAS. For this model, psi represents the difference in feature intensity resulting from a simultaneous, one-quantile increase of all PFAS in the mixture </li>
  <li>*SE*: standard error </li>
  <li>*ci_lower*: lower 95% confidence interval</li>
  <li>*ci_upper*: upper 95% confidence interval</li>
  <li>*p.value*: unadjusted p-value (before FDR correction)</li> 
  <li>*mode*: negative (C18) or positive (HILIC)</li> 
  <li>*FDR*: false discovery rate (FDR) corrected p-value</li>
</div>
<br>

**For the code below, you will need to specify your own file pathways to export the results. Furthermore, if you are adjusting for covariates, you will need to update the variables in the model.** As a reminder, all PFAS have already been log2 transformed. *value* in this code refers to the ion abundance of each feature.

```{r Linear_PFAS}
# Creating the function
find_linear_pfas <- function(list, PFAS) {
  num_metabolites <- length(list)
  res_mat <- matrix(NA, nrow = num_metabolites, ncol = 8) 
  colnames(res_mat) <- c("m.z", "r.t", "Beta", "SE", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p.value", "mode")
  for (i in 1:num_metabolites) {
    data_matrix <- as.matrix(list[[i]])
    # Fitting linear regression model with specified PFAS
    formula_str <- paste0("value ~ ", PFAS, " + midincome + mom_race + momagedeliv + ct_16w + parity")
    res <- lm(as.formula(formula_str), data = list[[i]])
    # Filling in results matrix
    res_mat[i, 1] <- as.numeric(list[[i]][1, 2]) #mz
    res_mat[i, 2] <- as.numeric(list[[i]][1, 3]) #time
    res_mat[i, 3] <- res$coefficients[PFAS] #Beta estimate
    res_mat[i, 4] <- summary(res)$coefficients[PFAS, "Std. Error"] #standard error
    res_mat[i, 5:6] <- confint(res, PFAS, level = 0.95) #upper and lower confidence interval
    res_mat[i, 7] <- summary(res)$coefficients[PFAS, "Pr(>|t|)"] #p-value
    res_mat[i, 8] <- as.numeric(list[[i]][1, 4]) #mode (i.e. direction)
  }
  # Converting matrix to data frame and add FDR column
  res_df <- as.data.frame(res_mat)
  colnames(res_df) <- colnames(res_mat)
  res_df$FDR <- p.adjust(res_df$p.value, method = 'BH')
  # Recoding mode column
  res_df$mode[res_df$mode == 1] <- "negative" #C18
  res_df$mode[res_df$mode == 2] <- "positive" #HILIC
  #Returns your wanted values
  return(res_df)
}
# Creating the datafiles
  # PFOA
  PFOA_Full <- find_linear_pfas(split_pfas, "pfoa_log2")
  PFOA_SIG <- PFOA_Full[PFOA_Full$FDR< 0.2,]
  PFOA_METABOANALYST <- subset(PFOA_Full, select=c("m.z", "p.value","r.t", "mode"))
  
  # PFOS
  PFOS_Full <- find_linear_pfas(split_pfas, "pfos_log2")
  PFOS_SIG <- PFOS_Full[PFOS_Full$FDR< 0.2,]
  PFOS_METABOANALYST <- subset(PFOS_Full, select=c("m.z", "p.value","r.t", "mode"))
  
  # PFNA
  PFNA_Full <- find_linear_pfas(split_pfas, "pfna_log2")
  PFNA_SIG <- PFNA_Full[PFNA_Full$FDR< 0.2,]
  PFNA_METABOANALYST <- subset(PFNA_Full, select=c("m.z", "p.value","r.t", "mode"))
  
  # PFHxS
  PFHxS_Full <- find_linear_pfas(split_pfas, "pfhxs_log2")
  PFHxS_SIG <- PFHxS_Full[PFHxS_Full$FDR< 0.2,]
  PFHxS_METABOANALYST <- subset(PFHxS_Full, select=c("m.z", "p.value","r.t", "mode"))
  
  # MEFOSAA
  MEFOSAA_Full <- find_linear_pfas(split_pfas, "me_pfosa_acoh_log2")
  MEFOSAA_SIG <- MEFOSAA_Full[MEFOSAA_Full$FDR< 0.2,]
  MEFOSAA_METABOANALYST <- subset(MEFOSAA_Full, select=c("m.z", "p.value","r.t", "mode"))
```

```{r QGComp_PFAS_MeFOSAA}
# Create a exposure list of the names of each of the 5 PFAS
Xnm <- c("pfoa_log2","pfos_log2","pfna_log2","pfhxs_log2", "me_pfosa_acoh_log2")

# Writing a function that loops through each individual features and runs quantile-based g-computation, adjusting for covariates.
find_psi_4PFAS_and_ME_PFOSA <- function(list) {
  num_metabolites <- length(list)
  res_mat <- matrix(NA, nrow = num_metabolites, ncol = 8)
  colnames(res_mat) <- c("m.z", "r.t", "psi", "SE", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p.value", "mode")
  for (i in 1:num_metabolites) {
    data_matrix <- as.matrix(list[[i]])
    # Quantile G-comp model
    res <- qgcomp.noboot(value ~ midincome + mom_race + momagedeliv + ct_16w + parity +
                           pfoa_log2 + pfos_log2 + pfna_log2 + pfhxs_log2 + 
                           me_pfosa_acoh_log2,
                         expnms = Xnm, data = list[[i]], family = gaussian())
    # Outputting needed values
    res_mat[i, 1] <- as.numeric(list[[i]][1, 2]) # mz
    res_mat[i, 2] <- as.numeric(list[[i]][1, 3]) # time ie. r.t
    res_mat[i, 3] <- as.numeric(res$psi) # psi
    res_mat[i,4] <- as.numeric((res$ci[2]-res$ci[1])/3.92) #SE
    res_mat[i, 5:6] <- res$ci # upper and lower confidence interval
    res_mat[i, 7] <- as.numeric(res$pval[2]) # p-value
    res_mat[i, 8] <- as.numeric(list[[i]][1, 4]) # mode
  }
  # Applying the FDR correction
  res_df <- data.frame(res_mat)
  res_df$FDR <- p.adjust(res_df$p.value, method = 'BH')
  # Recoding mode to 'megative' and 'positive'
  res_df$mode[res_df$mode == 1] <- "negative"
  res_df$mode[res_df$mode == 2] <- "positive"
  return(res_df)
}
# Creating files
qg_comp_5_FULL <- suppressWarnings(as.data.frame(find_psi_4PFAS_and_ME_PFOSA(split_pfas)))
qg_comp_5_SIG <- qg_comp_5_FULL[qg_comp_5_FULL$FDR< 0.2,]
qg_comp_5_METABOANALYST <- subset(qg_comp_5_FULL, select=c("m.z", "p.value","r.t", "mode"))
```

<h2 style="text-align: center"> **3. Pathway Enrichment Analysis** </h2>

<h3 style="text-align: center"> 3.0. Brief Background: MetaboanalystR </h3>

MetaboAnalystR is the R package associated with MetaboAnalyst. MetaboAnalystR performs a pathway enrichment analysis (PEA) using *mummichog* to identify associations between an exposure of interest, such as PFAS, and metabolic pathways. More information on *mummichog* can be found here [(Li et al.)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23861661/).   
<br>
Furthermore, information on the theory behind Metaboanalyst can be found here [(MetaboAnalyst)](https://www.metaboanalyst.ca/). Information on MetaboAnalystR (coding Metaboanalyst in R specifically) can be found at [(MetaboanalystR)](https://www.metaboanalyst.ca/docs/RTutorial.xhtml).

<h3 style="text-align: center"> 3.1. Adduct Specification </h3>

For the PEA, I first specify the adducts permitted for this study. This determination was made by our lead chemist Dr. Kate Manz. The purpose of adduct restriction is to restrict results to the adducts that could potentially form based on mobile phases and internal standards. As such, this may differ from study to study. 

A full list of the adducts available for MetaboAnalyst can be found here [(adduct list)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jsychong/MetaboAnalystR/master/mixed_add_list.txt).

```{r Adduct_Customization}
# Creating a vector that contains the customized adducts for this study. 
add.vec <- c("M+FA-H [1-]","M-H [1-]","2M-H [1-]","M-H+O [1-]","M(C13)-H [1-]",
             "2M+FA-H [1-]","M-3H [3-]","M-2H [2-]","M+ACN-H [1-]",
             "M+HCOO [1-]","M+CH3COO [1-]","M-H2O-H [1-]","M [1+]","M+H [1+]",
             "M+2H [2+]","M+3H [3+]","M+H2O+H [1+]","M-H2O+H [1+]",
             "M(C13)+H [1+]","M(C13)+2H [2+]","M(C13)+3H [3+]","M-NH3+H [1+]",
             "M+ACN+H [1+]","M+ACN+2H [2+]","M+2ACN+2H [2+]","M+3ACN+2H [2+]",
             "M+NH4 [1+]","M+H+NH4 [2+]","2M+H [1+]","2M+ACN+H [1+]")
```

<h3 style="text-align: center"> 3.2. 4-PFAS Mixture PEA</h3>

Using the results from the 4-PFAS Mixture MWAS (Section 2.1), I conducted a *mummichog* PEA to identify enriched pathways using MetaboAnalystR. 

Details regarding the untargeted analysis are described in detail in my first author paper  [(Hall et al.)](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acs.est.3c07515). From this information, I restricted to adducts that could potentially form based on mobile phases and internal standards (the specific adducts used in this analyses are detailed in the box below). This PEA was conducted using the human MFN network, a mass tolerance of 5ppm, 10,000 permutations and a p-value cutoff <0.05 to delineate between significantly enriched and non-significantly enriched features. Furthermore, this analysis was restricted to metabolite data sets containing at least 3 entries. A p(gamma) < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.  
<br>

<div style="border: 1px solid #000; padding: 10px; text-align: center">
<h5 style="text-align: center"> **Adducts I Restricted to in This Analyses**</h5> 
  <p><u>Negative Ion Mode</u></p>
  <p>M+FA-H [1-], M-H [1-], 2M-H [1-], M-H2O-H [1-], M-H+O [1-], M(C13)-H [1-], 2M+FA-H [1-], M-3H [3-], M-2H [2-], M+ACN-H [1-], M+HCOO[1-], and M+CH3COO [1-]</p>
  <p><u>Positive Ion Mode</u></p>
  <p>M [1+], M+H [1+], M+2H [2+], M+3H [3+], M+H2O+H [1+], M-H2O+H [1+], M(C13)+H [1+], M(C13)+2H [2+], M(C13)+3H [3+], M-NH3+H [1+], M+ACN+H [1+], M+ACN+2H [2+], M+2ACN+2H [2+], M+3ACN+2H [2+], M+NH4 [1+], M+H+NH4 [2+], 2M+H [1+], and 2M+ACN+H [1+]</p>
</div>
<br>
**You will need to specify your own file pathways to export the results. The files imported for this analysis were created and exported out in Section 2.1.**

```{r PEA_4PFAS, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}
# Creating an object for storing data for mummichog
mSet4 <- MetaboAnalystR::InitDataObjects("mass_all", "mummichog", FALSE, default.dpi = 72)

# Ranking the peaks by their p-value
mSet4 <- SetPeakFormat(mSet4, "rmp") 

# Specifying
    #a. a mass tolerance of 5.0
    #b. mixed mode
    #c.not enforcing primary ions as this is exploratory
mSet4 <- UpdateInstrumentParameters(mSet4, 5.0, "mixed", "no"); 

# Reading in the specific peak list
mSet4 <- Read.PeakListData(mSet4, "Final Datasets/Metaboanalyst/QG_comp_full_METABOLOMICS_4PFAS.csv"); # INSERT YOUR PATHWAY HERE

# Performing a sanity check to ensure the data is in a suitable format for further analysis
mSet4 <- SanityCheckMummichogData(mSet4)

# Adding in the adduct data
mSet4 <- Setup.AdductData(mSet4, add.vec); 

# Specifying both positive and negative adducts
mSet4 <- PerformAdductMapping(mSet4, "mixed") 

# Running the mummichog algorithm using selected adducts and version 2 of the mummichog algorithm
mSet4 <- SetPeakEnrichMethod(mSet4, "mum", "v2")
mSet4 <- SetMummichogPval(mSet4, .05) #Specifying a p-value of 0.05

# Selecting the human MFN network, selecting the current human MFN library, restricting to metabolite datasets with at least 3 entries, and running 10,000 permutations. 
mSet4 <- PerformPSEA(mSet4, "hsa_mfn", "current", 3 , 10000)

# Storing the results as a dataframe
mummi_results_4pfas <- as.data.frame(mSet4$mummi.resmat)

# Restricting the results to those with a p(gamma) <0.05
mummi_results_4pfas <- mummi_results_4pfas[mummi_results_4pfas$Gamma< 0.05, ]
```

<h3 style="text-align: center"> 3.3. Single Pollutant PEA </h3>

Using the results from the single pollutant MWAS models (Section 2.2), I conducted a *mummichog* PEA to identify enriched pathways using MetaboAnalystR. This was part of a secondary analysis that evaluated the impact of individual PFAS on the PEA of the 4-PFAS mixture (this is discussed in Section 3.2).

Details regarding the untargeted analysis are described in detail in my first author paper  [(Hall et al.)](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acs.est.3c07515). From this information, I restricted to adducts that could potentially form based on mobile phases and internal standards (the specific adducts used in this analyses are detailed in the box below). This PEA was conducted using the human MFN network, a mass tolerance of 5ppm, 10,000 permutations and a p-value cutoff <0.05 to delineate between significantly enriched and non-significantly enriched features. Furthermore, this analysis was restricted to metabolite data sets containing at least 3 entries. A p(gamma) < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.  

<div style="border: 1px solid #000; padding: 10px; text-align: center;">
  <p><strong>Adducts I Restricted to in This Analyses</strong></p>
  <p><u>Negative Ion Mode</u></p>
  <p>M+FA-H [1-], M-H [1-], 2M-H [1-], M-H2O-H [1-], M-H+O [1-], M(C13)-H [1-], 2M+FA-H [1-], M-3H [3-], M-2H [2-], M+ACN-H [1-], M+HCOO [1-], and M+CH3COO [1-]</p>
  <p><u>Positive Ion Mode</u></p>
  <p>M [1+], M+H [1+], M+2H [2+], M+3H [3+], M+H2O+H [1+], M-H2O+H [1+], M(C13)+H [1+], M(C13)+2H [2+], M(C13)+3H [3+], M-NH3+H [1+], M+ACN+H [1+], M+ACN+2H [2+], M+2ACN+2H [2+], M+3ACN+2H [2+], M+NH4 [1+], M+H+NH4 [2+], 2M+H [1+], and 2M+ACN+H [1+]</p>
</div>
<br>

**You will need to specify your own file pathways to export the results. The files imported for this analysis were created and exported out in Section 2.2.**

```{r PEA_Individual_PFAS, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}
# Creating a list of the PFAS we are evaluating
PFAS <- c("PFOA", "PFOS", "PFHxS", "PFNA", "MEFOSAA")

# Creating an empty list to store the results for each PFAS
results_list <- list()

# Creating a loop to loop through each PFAS and output the results
for (PFAS in PFAS) {
  # Creating an object for storing data for mummichog
  mSet <- InitDataObjects("mass_all", "mummichog", FALSE, default.dpi = 72)
  # Ranking the peaks by their p-value
  mSet <- SetPeakFormat(mSet, "rmp")
  # Specifying instrument parameters
  mSet <- UpdateInstrumentParameters(mSet, 5.0, "mixed", "no")
  # Reading in the specific peak list
  file_path <- paste("Final Datasets/Metaboanalyst/Individual PFAS/", PFAS, "_METABOANALYST.csv", sep = "")
  mSet <- Read.PeakListData(mSet, file_path)
  # Performing a sanity check
  mSet <- SanityCheckMummichogData(mSet)
  # Adding in the adduct data
  mSet <- Setup.AdductData(mSet, add.vec)
  # Specifying both positive and negative adducts
  mSet <- PerformAdductMapping(mSet, "mixed")
  # Running the mummichog algorithm using selected adducts and version 2 of the mummichog algorithm
  mSet <- SetPeakEnrichMethod(mSet, "mum", "v2")
  mSet <- SetMummichogPval(mSet, 0.05) # Specifying a p-value of 0.05
  # Selecting the human MFN network, selecting the current human MFN library, restricting to metabolite datasets with at least 3 entries, and running 10,000 permutations
  mSet <- PerformPSEA(mSet, "hsa_mfn", "current", 3, 10000)
  # Storing the results as a dataframe
  results_list[[PFAS]] <- as.data.frame(mSet$mummi.resmat)
  # Restricting the results to those with a p(gamma) < 0.05
  results_list[[PFAS]] <- results_list[[PFAS]][results_list[[PFAS]]$Gamma < 0.05, ]
}
```

<h3 style="text-align: center"> 3.4. Sensitivity PEA (5-PFAS) </h3>

Using the results from the 5-PFAS Mixture MWAS (Section 2.3), I conducted a *mummichog* PEA to identify enriched pathways using MetaboAnalystR. This was a sensitivity analysis to determine the impact of MeFOSAA on the PEA of the 4-PFAS mixture (this is discussed in Section 3.2). 

Details regarding the untargeted analysis are described in detail in my first author paper  [(Hall et al.)](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acs.est.3c07515). From this information, I restricted to adducts that could potentially form based on mobile phases and internal standards (the specific adducts used in this analyses are detailed in the box below). This PEA was conducted using the human MFN network, a mass tolerance of 5ppm, 10,000 permutations and a p-value cutoff <0.05 to delineate between significantly enriched and non-significantly enriched features. Furthermore, this analysis was restricted to metabolite data sets containing at least 3 entries. A p(gamma) < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.   

<div style="border: 1px solid #000; padding: 10px; text-align: center;">
  <p><strong>Adducts Restricted to in This Analyses</strong></p>
  <p><u>Negative Ion Mode</u></p>
  <p>M+FA-H [1-], M-H [1-], 2M-H [1-], M-H2O-H [1-], M-H+O [1-], M(C13)-H [1-], 2M+FA-H [1-], M-3H [3-], M-2H [2-], M+ACN-H [1-], M+HCOO [1-], and M+CH3COO [1-]</p>
  <p><u>Positive Ion Mode</u></p>
  <p>M [1+], M+H [1+], M+2H [2+], M+3H [3+], M+H2O+H [1+], M-H2O+H [1+], M(C13)+H [1+], M(C13)+2H [2+], M(C13)+3H [3+], M-NH3+H [1+], M+ACN+H [1+], M+ACN+2H [2+], M+2ACN+2H [2+], M+3ACN+2H [2+], M+NH4 [1+], M+H+NH4 [2+], 2M+H [1+], and 2M+ACN+H [1+]</p>
</div>
<br>
**You will need to specify your own file pathways to export the results. The files imported for this analysis were created and exported out in Section 2.3.**

```{r PEA_5PFAS, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}
# Creating an object for storing data for mummichog
mSet5 <- InitDataObjects("mass_all", "mummichog", FALSE, default.dpi = 72)

# Ranking the peaks by thei p-value
mSet5<- SetPeakFormat(mSet5, "rmp") 

# Specifying
    #a. a mass tolerance of 5.0
    #b. mixed mode
    #c. not enforcing primary ions. 
mSet5<-UpdateInstrumentParameters(mSet5, 5.0, "mixed", "no"); 

# Reading in the specific peak list
mSet5<-Read.PeakListData(mSet5, "Final Datasets/Metaboanalyst/QG_comp_full_METABOLOMICS_4PFAS_and_ME_PFOSA.csv"); # INSERT YOUR PATHWAY HERE

# Performing a sanity check to ensure the data is in a suitable format for further analysis
mSet5<-SanityCheckMummichogData(mSet5)

# Adding in the adduct data
mSet5<-Setup.AdductData(mSet5, add.vec); 

# Specifying both positive and negative adducts
mSet5<-PerformAdductMapping(mSet5, "mixed") 

# Running the mummichog algorithm using selected adducts and version 2 of the mummichog algorithm
mSet5<-SetPeakEnrichMethod(mSet5, "mum", "v2")
mSet5<-SetMummichogPval(mSet5, .05) #Specifying a p-value of 0.05

# Selecting the human MFN network, selecting the current human MFN library, restricting to metabolite datasets with at least 3 entries, and running 10,000 permutations. 
mSet5<-PerformPSEA(mSet5, "hsa_mfn", "current", 3 , 10000)

# Storing the results as a dataframe
mummi_results_5pfas<- as.data.frame(mSet5$mummi.resmat)

# Restricting the results to those with a p(gamma) <0.05
mummi_results_5pfas <- mummi_results_5pfas[mummi_results_5pfas$Gamma< 0.05, ]
```

<h1 style="text-align: center"> **Figures and Table Code** </h1>
Below is the code I used to generate many of the figures and the descriptive table presented in my first-author, peer-reviewed publication <a href="https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acs.est.3c07515" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">(Hall et al.)</a>. This section is intended to serve both as a practical guide for people to understand, adapt, or extend these analyses. For ease of navigation, the code is organized into three main sections, corresponding to the major figure types and analytic stages of the study. These sections are detailed under 'Workflow & Deliverables'. 

<h2 style="text-align: center"> **4. Exploratory Data Analysis** </h2>
<h3 style="text-align: center"> 4.1. PFAS Correlation Heatmap </h3>

In order to better understand the relationships among the different PFAS exposures (PFOS, PFOA, PFNA, PFHxS, and MeFOSAA), I created a heatmap summarizing pairwise correlations. This heatmap displays Spearman correlation coefficients calculated using non–log-transformed PFAS concentrations.

Spearman correlations were chosen because the non-transformed PFAS distributions were not normally distributed, making Pearson correlations less appropriate. Spearman’s rank-based approach does not rely on distributional assumptions and is therefore more robust to skewed exposure data. That said, Pearson correlations using log-transformed PFAS concentrations would also be a reasonable alternative and yield complementary information.

To generate this figure, I imported the non-transformed PFAS dataset, selected the relevant exposure variables, and computed pairwise Spearman correlation coefficients, which were then visualized as a heatmap.
```{r Heatmap1}
# Importing the file containing the non-transformed pfas data
full_cov_pfas <- read.csv("Data/pfas_not_transformed.csv") # INSERT YOUR DATA HERE

# Selecting specific columns
cor_cols <- dplyr::select(full_cov_pfas, PFOA, PFNA, PFHxS, PFOS, MeFOSAA)

# Calculating correlation matrix and rounding off the values
cormat <- round(cor(cor_cols, method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs"), 2)
```
<br>
After calculating the Spearman correlation coefficients, I created the heatmap using this code:
```{r Heatmap2}
# Keep upper triangle only (blank out lower triangle)
cormat[lower.tri(cormat)] <- NA

# Melting the correlation matrix and removing NA values
melted_cormat <- melt(cormat, na.rm = TRUE)
melted_cormat$value <- as.numeric(melted_cormat$value)

# Creating a heatmap of Spearman Correlation coefficients
spearman_cor <- ggplot(data = melted_cormat, aes(Var2, Var1, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", high = "red", mid = "white", 
                      midpoint = 0, limit = c(-1, 1), space = "Lab", 
                      name = "Spearman\nCorrelation") +
  labs(title = paste(
      strwrap("Figure 1. Spearman correlation coefficients between maternal serum PFAS in the HOME Study (2003 to 2006; N = 264)", width = 70), collapse = "\n"), x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      hjust = 0.4,   
      size = 13,
      family = "Times New Roman"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, size = 12, hjust = 1, family = "Times New Roman"), 
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0, family = "Times New Roman"), 
        axis.title.x = element_blank(),  
        axis.title.y = element_blank(), 
        legend.text = element_text(family = "Times New Roman"), 
        legend.title = element_text(family = "Times New Roman"), 
        panel.grid.major = element_blank(), 
        panel.border = element_blank(), 
        panel.background = element_blank(), 
        axis.ticks = element_blank(), 
        legend.justification = c(1, 0), 
        legend.position = c(0.4, 0.7), 
        legend.direction = "horizontal") +
  coord_fixed() + 
  geom_text(aes(Var2, Var1, label = value), color = "black", size = 4, family = "Times New Roman") +
  guides(fill = guide_colorbar(barwidth = 7, barheight = 1, 
                               title.position = "top", title.hjust = 0.5)) +
  scale_y_discrete(position = "right")

print(spearman_cor)
```

<h3 style="text-align: center"> 4.2. PFAS Violin Plots </h3>

In my published first-author paper, PFAS distributions were summarized in a table rather than shown graphically. This decision was made as the spread of their concentrations differ substantially, making PFNA, PFHxS, and MeFOSAA difficult to read. However, I provide this code for readers who prefer a visual representation of PFAS distributions or who wish to adapt the plotting workflow for their own analyses.

To summarize the distributions of prenatal PFAS concentrations, I used violin plots. Violin plots display the full distribution of each PFAS, allowing comparison of distributional patterns across compounds without grouping or binning the data. I overlay the violin plots with box plots to provide a compact summary of the median and interquartile range. Because PFAS concentrations differ substantially in scale across compounds in my study, I also include a median (IQR) table beneath the figure to ensure that PFAS with smaller concentration ranges remain interpretable.
```{r Violin_Plots}
# Note. This plot uses the non–log-transformed PFAS data that were previously imported for the correlation heatmap. The corresponding data import step is commented out below and provided for reference and reuse.

# Importing the file containing the non-transformed pfas data
#full_cov_pfas <- read.csv("Data/pfas_not_transformed.csv") # INSERT YOUR DATA HERE

# Assigning colors to each PFAS
pfas_colors <- c(
  "PFOA" = "#3C8DC4",
  "PFNA" = "#FF9A3F",
  "PFHxS" = "#942E2E",
  "PFOS" = "hotpink",
  "MeFOSAA" = "black")

# Calculating the median (IQR) for each PFAS. This will provide a table at the bottom of my violin plots with medians and IQR for each PFAS.  
pfas_medians <- full_cov_pfas %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = names(pfas_colors),
    names_to = "Chemical",
    values_to = "Concentration") %>%
  dplyr::group_by(Chemical) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    Median = round(median(Concentration, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Q1     = round(stats::quantile(Concentration, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Q3     = round(stats::quantile(Concentration, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(Median_IQR = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", Median, Q1, Q3))

# Reversing the order so it presents from high to low
PFAS_order <- rev(pfas_medians$Chemical)

# Reshaping the data
pfas_long <- full_cov_pfas %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = names(pfas_colors), names_to = "Chemical", values_to = "Concentration") %>%
  mutate(Chemical = factor(Chemical, levels = PFAS_order))

# Creating a table to display under the plot with median and IQR
table_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_text(data = pfas_medians,
    aes(x = Chemical, y = 0, label = "Median (IQR)"),
    size = 4.5, hjust = 0.5, vjust = -0.5,
    fontface = "bold", family = "Times") +
  geom_text(data = pfas_medians,
    aes(x = Chemical, y = 0, label = Median_IQR),
    size = 4, hjust = 0.5, vjust = 1,
    family = "Times") +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = PFAS_order) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0, "cm"))

# Making the violin plot + boxplot overlay (cap y-axis at 30)
violin_plot <- ggplot(pfas_long, aes(x = Chemical, y = Concentration, fill = Chemical)) +
  geom_violin(trim = FALSE, scale = "width", adjust = 1.2, color = "black") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.4, fill = "white", alpha = 0.4, outlier.shape = NA, color = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pfas_colors) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = expression(bold("Concentration (ng/mL)"))) +
  labs(title = paste(
      strwrap("Figure 2. Concentrations of maternal serum PFAS in the HOME Study (2003 to 2006; N = 264)", width = 70), collapse = "\n"), x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", color = "black", family = "Times"),
    axis.text.x  = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", color = "black", family = "Times"),
    axis.text.y  = element_text(size = 12, color = "black", family = "Times"),
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x.bottom = element_line(linewidth = 0.5, color = "black"),
    axis.line.y.left = element_line(linewidth = 0.5, color = "black"),
    axis.ticks.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.5, color = "black"),
    axis.ticks.length = unit(0.2, "cm"),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = NA, color = "white"),
    plot.title = element_text(
    face   = "bold",
    size   = 13,
    family = "Times",
    hjust  = 0.4))
# Combining with the median (IQR) table with my violin plot
final_violin <- ggarrange(violin_plot, table_plot, ncol = 1, heights = c(4, 1))
print(final_violin)
```

<h3 style="text-align: center"> 4.3. Study Characteristics Table </h3>
Table 1 summarizes maternal and household characteristics for participants included in the HOME Study cohort (2003–2006). Descriptive statistics were calculated using the full covariate dataset to reflect the underlying study population, consistent with standard epidemiologic reporting practices.

Continuous variables are presented as medians with interquartile ranges (IQR) to account for skewed distributions, while categorical variables are summarized using counts and percentages calculated among non-missing observations. Key characteristics include maternal age at delivery, race/ethnicity, gestational tobacco exposure (measured via cotinine concentrations at approximately 16 weeks’ gestation), household income, and parity.

This table serves to contextualize the cohort prior to downstream metabolome-wide analyses. A thorough evaluation of covariate functional forms (including assessment of linearity and alternative parameterizations) was conducted separately and is described outside of this descriptive section.
```{r Covariate_Table, results='asis', echo=TRUE}
# Note. This plot uses the non–log-transformed PFAS data that were previously imported for the correlation heatmap. The corresponding data import step is commented out below and provided for reference and reuse.

# Importing the file containing the non-transformed pfas data
#full_cov_pfas <- read.csv("Data/pfas_not_transformed.csv") # INSERT YOUR DATA HERE

# Creating the sample size used for Table 1
N <- nrow(full_cov_pfas)

# Formatting continuous variables as Median [IQR]
med_iqr <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  sprintf(
    paste0("%.", digits, "f [%.", digits, "f–%.", digits, "f]"),
    median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    stats::quantile(x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    stats::quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE))
}

# Formatting categorical variables as N (%), excluding missing values from the denominator
n_pct <- function(cond) {
  n <- sum(cond, na.rm = TRUE)
  p <- mean(cond, na.rm = TRUE) * 100
  sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", n, p)
}

# Creating the Table 1 structure (row labels + formatted summaries)
table1 <- tibble::tibble(
  Characteristic = c(
    "Number of participants",
    "Maternal age at delivery (years)",
    "Maternal race/ethnicity: White, non-Hispanic",
    "Maternal race/ethnicity: Other race/ethnicity",
    "Cotinine at ~16 weeks (ng/mL)",
    "Annual household income < $20,000",
    "Annual household income $20,000–$40,000",
    "Annual household income $40,000–$80,000",
    "Annual household income > $80,000",
    "Parity: Nulliparous",
    "Parity: Parous"),
  `N (%) or Median [IQR]` = c(as.character(N),
    med_iqr(full_cov_pfas$momagedeliv, digits = 1),
    n_pct(full_cov_pfas$mom_race == "White, non-Hispanic"),
    n_pct(full_cov_pfas$mom_race != "White, non-Hispanic" & !is.na(full_cov_pfas$mom_race)),
    med_iqr(full_cov_pfas$ct_16w, digits = 3),
    n_pct(full_cov_pfas$midincome < 20000),
    n_pct(full_cov_pfas$midincome >= 20000 & full_cov_pfas$midincome < 40000),
    n_pct(full_cov_pfas$midincome >= 40000 & full_cov_pfas$midincome <= 80000),
    n_pct(full_cov_pfas$midincome > 80000),
    n_pct(full_cov_pfas$parity == "Nulliparous"),
    n_pct(full_cov_pfas$parity == "Parous")))

# Creating the table
base_css  <- "font-family: Times; color: black; background-color: white;"
title_css <- "font-family: Times; color: black; font-size: 1.15em;"
table_title <- "Table 1. Maternal characteristics among participants in the HOME Study (2003 to 2006)"
knitr::kable(table1,
  format = "html",
  escape = TRUE,
  table.attr = "style='background-color: white; width: 60%; margin-left: 0;'") |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    full_width = FALSE,
    position   = "center",
    font_size  = 15) |>
  # Adding the title as a header row
kableExtra::add_header_above(setNames(2, table_title),
  bold = TRUE,
  background = "white",
  extra_css = title_css) |>
  # Setting column widths (adjust as needed)
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, width = "66%", extra_css = base_css) |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(2, width = "34%", extra_css = base_css) |>
  # Forcing Times + black text + white fill everywhere
  kableExtra::row_spec(0, background = "white", extra_css = base_css) |>
  kableExtra::row_spec(1:nrow(table1), background = "white", extra_css = base_css)
```

<h2 style="text-align: center"> **5. Metabolome-Wide Association Study- Figures** </h2>
For the metabolome-wide association study (MWAS), volcano plots were used to screen thousands of metabolomic features and highlight those with both the largest estimated associations with prenatal PFAS exposure (effect size) and the strongest statistical evidence after multiple-testing correction. This visualization facilitates rapid prioritization of candidate metabolites for downstream annotation and pathway enrichment by jointly displaying magnitude of association and statistical significance.

To account for the large number of simultaneous tests inherent to MWAS, statistical significance was evaluated using the Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) procedure to control the false discovery rate (FDR), defined as the expected proportion of false positives among features identified as significant. BH was selected because it provides principled error control while preserving power in high-dimensional discovery settings such as metabolomics, where more conservative family-wise error approaches (e.g., Bonferroni) can be overly restrictive.

An FDR threshold of 0.20 was used to emphasize discovery and candidate prioritization rather than definitive inference, with the goal of carrying forward a manageable subset of features for downstream annotation and pathway enrichment.

For visualization, a horizontal FDR significance threshold was drawn in red on each volcano plot and defined as:
\[\begin{aligned}\small\left(\frac{\text{number of significant values}}{\text{number of total values}}\right)\times 0.2\end{aligned}\]

This was then transformed to the -log10 scale for visualization. Features exceeding this p<0.20 threshold (with BH correction) are highlighted in red to distinguish statistically prioritized metabolites from the background distribution.

<h3 style="text-align: center"> 5.1. 4-PFAS mixture volcano plot </h3>

For the 4-PFAS mixture, a volcano plot was created to display metabolome-wide association results for the joint effect of prenatal exposure to the four PFAS compounds. Each point represents a metabolomic feature, plotted by its estimated effect size (log2-fold change in ion intensity) on the x-axis and the strength of statistical evidence on the y-axis (-log10 scale)
```{r 4-PFAS-Volcano}
# Calculating the number of significant values for the 4-PFAS mixture
n_sig_4 = nrow(qg_comp_4_SIG)
# Calculating the total number of values in the 4-PFAS analysis
n_total_4 = nrow(qg_comp_4_FULL)

# Converting an FDR=0.20–scaled p-value cutoff (0.2 × proportion significant) into the volcano plot y-value (-log10 p) for the horizontal “significance” line.
threshold <- -log10(n_sig_4 /n_total_4 * 0.2) #(significant/total N)*p-value

# Creating the volcano plot for the 4-PFAS mixture
pfas_mwas <- ggplot() +
# Adding grey points below the line
geom_point(data = subset(qg_comp_4_FULL, -log10(p.value) <= threshold), aes(x = psi, y = -log10(p.value)), color = "darkgray") +
  # Adding red points to better identify significant values (above the line)
  geom_point(data = subset(qg_comp_4_FULL, -log10(p.value) > threshold), aes(x = psi, y = -log10(p.value)), color = "red") +
  # Adding a horizontal line to denote significance threshold
  geom_hline(yintercept = threshold, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  # Adding labels and titles
  labs(title = paste(strwrap("Figure 3. Cord blood metabolic features associated with a mixture of 4 PFAS during gestation in the HOME Study (2003 to 2006, N = 264)", width = 70), collapse = "\n"), 
       x = "Log2-Fold Change in Ion Intensity",
       y = "-Log10 (p-value)") +
  # Applying a black and white theme
  theme_bw() +
  # Modifying the theme to remove x-axis grid lines and set font and axis color
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), 
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(family = "Times"),
    axis.text = element_text(colour = "black"),
    axis.ticks = element_line(colour = "black"),
    plot.title = element_text(face   = "bold", size   = 13, family = "Times", hjust  = 0.4))

# Printing the plot
print(pfas_mwas)
```
<h3 style="text-align: center"> 5.2. Single-PFAS volcano plots </h3>
To examine compound-specific associations, volcano plots were generated separately for each of the four individual PFAS included in the mixture. Each plot displays metabolomic features by estimated effect size and statistical significance, allowing direct comparison of association patterns across compounds.

The individual volcano plots were created using a consistent modeling and visualization framework and then combined into a single figure using the ggpubr package to facilitate side-by-side comparison. The code for each individual plot and its corresponding output are shown below.

<h4 style="text-align: center"> 5.2.1 Single-PFAS volcano plots:PFOA (Plot 1 of 4)</h4>
```{r Single-PFAS-Volcano-PFOA}
# Calculating the number of significant values for the PFOA MWAS
n_sig_PFOA = nrow(PFOA_SIG)
# Calculating the total number of values in the PFOA MWAS
n_total_PFOA = nrow(PFOA_Full)

# Converts an FDR=0.20–scaled p-value cutoff (0.2 × proportion significant) into the volcano plot y-value (-log10 p) for the horizontal “significance” line.
threshold <- -log10(n_sig_PFOA /n_total_PFOA * 0.2) #(significant/total N)*p-value

# Creating the volcano plot for PFOA
pfoa_mwas_plot <- ggplot() +
  # Adding grey points below the line
  geom_point(
    data = subset(PFOA_Full, -log10(p.value) <=threshold), 
    aes(x = Beta, y = -log10(p.value)), 
    color = "darkgray") +
  # Adding red points above the line
  geom_point(
    data = subset(PFOA_Full, -log10(p.value) > threshold), 
    aes(x = Beta, y = -log10(p.value)), 
    color = "red") +
  # Adding a horizontal line to denote significance threshold
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = threshold, 
    color = "red", 
    linetype = "dashed") +
  # Adding labels and titles
  labs(
    x = "Log2-Fold Change in Ion Intensity", 
    y = "-Log10 (p-value)", 
    title = "a. PFOA") +
  # Applying a black and white theme
  theme_bw() +
  # Modifying the theme to remove x-axis grid lines and set font and axis color
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), 
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(family = 'Times'),
    axis.text = element_text(colour = "black"),
    axis.ticks = element_line(colour = "black"),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 11))
```
